children.translated_text: <s>Vīṇāśikhatantra</s>
Oṃ, salutation to the great <s>Bhairava</s>.
On the beautiful peak of <s>Kailāsa</s>,
adorned with various jewels,
filled with various trees and creepers,
attended by <s>Siddhas</s> and <s>Cāraṇas</s>,
there the god, the best of gods,
sports with <s>Umā</s>,
praised by the great <s>Siddhas</s>,
by the hosts headed by <s>Mahākāla</s>.
And by the great and blessed sages,
by <s>Bhṛgu</s> and others, the best of gods —
rising up from among them,
the <s>Devī</s> spoke these words:
"I have heard the <s>Sammohanatantra</s>,
and also the great <s>Nayottara</s>,
and the <s>Śiraścheda</s>, O Lord of Gods,
obtained through your grace, so difficult to obtain.
These are accomplished through observances,
and again through sacrificial rites;
since others in the world are dependent on other means
and generally lack material resources,
that which is superior even to these,
which grants <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment) through knowledge alone,
which bestows all desires, O God —
the five seed-syllables (<s>bījapañcaka</s>) as they truly are,
the supreme heart of these —
you should deign to give it to your devotee."
"That which has not been told to anyone,
not even to yogins such as <s>Śukra</s> and others,
which has been kept hidden from the devoted, the disciplined,
and even from <s>Guha</s> (Skanda),
the sixty-four disciples that I have
proclaimed in the <s>tantras</s> —
even to them it was not told,
even with <s>Brahmā</s> and <s>Viṣṇu</s> at the fore —
that I shall now declare,
like another wish-fulfilling gem:
the <s>tantra</s> called <s>Vīṇāśikha</s>,
which bestows swift accomplishment without deception.
United with <s>Devī</s> and <s>Tumburu</s>,
well-established upon the vīṇā-support,
they are desired by means of the topknot-yoga —
therefore it is called <s>Vīṇāśikhā</s>.
I shall first declare the sacrifice (<s>yāga</s>),
the essence of the <s>tantra</s>, so difficult to obtain;
by that very [rite], the goddesses become
perpetual boon-givers, O <s>Devī</s>.
This domestic sacrifice (<s>gṛhayāga</s>), O <s>Devī</s> —
the practitioner (<s>sādhaka</s>) who knows it here,
without observance or fire-oblation, in this [rite],
attains supreme <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment).
One should first perform the acceptance
of disciples, having performed the sacrifice;
one should not otherwise show the <s>tantra</s>,
nor shall that one attain <s>siddhi</s>.
On the fourth, or the fifth,
on the ninth, and on the eleventh [lunar days],
or during an eclipse it should be performed,
and always [on days of] the Sun and Moon.
Worship on the fourth is most excellent,
a great bestower of good fortune;
one desiring <s>Śrī</s> (prosperity) should perform worship
on the fifth, with a concentrated mind.
One desiring victory in battle,
or the subjugation of an enemy kingdom —
on the ninth, the royal sacrifice
should be performed, dear to the Sister.
One who worships on the eleventh
is exalted in <s>Śiva</s>'s world.
In a well-concealed, solitary place,
or on the bank of a river or pond,
having first purified the ground
with the <s>Sāvitrī</s> [mantra], the supreme teacher
should perform worship and then conduct
the consecration (<s>adhivāsana</s>) of the disciples.
Afterwards, for the ritual practice,
the wise one should have the <s>caru</s> (oblation) offered with the <s>Sāvitrī</s>;
and the tooth-stick for the disciples,
twelve finger-breadths long, with milk.
Having sipped water and called the disciple,
purified by the five principles (<s>pañcatattva</s>),
one should again sprinkle with the <s>Sāvitrī</s>,
recited over the principles, as prescribed.
One should sweep with the tip of <s>kuśa</s> grass
and touch the limbs of that one;
having touched with the <s>Sāvitrī</s>,
one should wash [each limb] completely, in order.
The disciples should sleep on the sacrificial ground
on a bed of <s>kuśa</s> grass,
always having made protection with a hundred seed-syllables,
having meditated upon them in order.
Then at the pure dawn,
the practitioner, having washed his face,
should prostrate before the teacher and report
the auspicious and inauspicious experiences [of the night].
Having learned the auspicious and inauspicious signs,
the teacher, for the practitioner,
first, on level ground in a place
that is secluded and free from thorns,
the wise one should draw a <s>maṇḍala</s>
properly, according to the prescribed method,
four cubits [square], with four doors,
or alternatively one cubit [square].
One should draw the divine <s>maṇḍala</s>,
radiant with rice flour;
in the middle thereof one should draw a lotus,
with four petals and a pericarp.
White, red, yellow, and black
are the petals of the lotus;
beginning from the east, in proper order,
one should draw [them ending with] the north and east [corners].
And in the middle, the pericarp,
the supreme teacher [should draw it] variegated;
with four forms and four colors,
<s>Tumburu</s>, with his own seed-syllable —
one should meditate upon the four-colored Lord
seated in the hollow of the pericarp;
then, with her own seed-syllable, the white
<s>Jayā</s> should be placed on the eastern petal.
Resembling the <s>bandhūka</s> flower,
<s>Vijayā</s> on the southern petal;
resembling pure gold,
<s>Ajitā</s> on the western petal;
resembling a mass of split collyrium,
<s>Aparājitā</s> on the northern [petal];
having placed [them], one should perform worship
with their respective seed-syllables, in order.
With flowers, incense, and offerings,
with auspicious items at the appropriate times;
the [ritual] enclosure adorned with fine canopies and banners,
decorated with garlands and flower-chains,
illuminated on all sides
by blazing lamps in [all] directions;
with various foods, rice preparations, and drinks,
and with delicious condiments,
with various kinds of fruits,
placed all around;
with water-pots filled with water,
stationed in the ten directions,
covered with mango-sprouts,
auspiciously adorned with garlands and flower-chains.
Having thus worshipped according to proper method,
having sprinkled the disciples with water,
bringing [them] face-to-face with the <s>Sāvitrī</s>,
blindfolded with cloth,
with their respective seed-syllables one should place flowers
in both hands of the disciples.
Through <s>Jayā</s>, the supreme teacher should cause entry
into the illusion (<s>māyā</s>) and the <s>maṇḍala</s>;
having led the disciple inside —
whether two, three, four, or five —
then one should perform the fire-rite
outside, to the west of the <s>maṇḍala</s>,
having drawn and raised up with the <s>Sāvitrī</s>,
and having spread <s>kuśa</s> grass all around.
Having sprinkled with the weapon-seed (<s>astrabīja</s>)
and scented water, the teacher
should take the fire and then
worship it with the <s>Sāvitrī</s>.
Then, having placed the three principles
upon the fire in proper order,
the <s>māyā</s> that has been restrained from that —
one should restrain it with the goad (<s>aṅkuśa</s>).
Afterwards, one should conceal with <s>māyā</s>,
and awaken with the weapon (<s>astra</s>) itself;
of all the oblation-materials,
one should perform purification with that very [mantra].
Then the wise one should have the oblation
of ghee performed according to proper method;
having offered with one's own seed-syllables,
one should perform the initiation (<s>dīkṣā</s>) of the disciple.
Having conjoined in proper order with the seed-syllables
in the five great elements,
having conjoined the <s>tattva</s> (principle) in the <s>sakala</s> (with parts),
having established it in the higher path,
one should then assign it there
where the vowel is supreme;
this is the initiation (<s>dīkṣā</s>), as is proper,
bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
By those very five [seed-syllables], the principle
in the <s>sakala</s> [state] is of the nature of <s>sakala</s>;
in the <s>niṣkala</s> (without parts) it is declared <s>niṣkala</s>,
pertaining to the authorized path, as before.
Having then initiated the disciples
who are established in the authorized higher [path],
having consecrated them with one's own seed-syllables,
one should bestow the seed-syllables upon them.
Having communicated the observances to that one,
through showing the heart, <s>mudrā</s>, and finger-gestures,
the permission of the chief practitioner
should be given to that one by the great soul.
Then the supreme practitioner should eat
the offering of his own <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge-mantra);
the goddesses become pleased indeed,
and the remainder should be cast into water.
One should worship the teacher with devotion,
with all [one's possessions] and in the highest manner;
with prostrations and gifts of ability,
or by whatever pleases the <s>guru</s>.
Wearing garlands, with a white turban,
adorned with all ornaments,
seated on a high seat, facing east,
one should arrange the grid-<s>maṇḍala</s> (<s>koṣamaṇḍala</s>).
Smeared with cow-dung ash,
in a clean place devoid of people,
on a level area of ground,
the pure one should lay out the grid (<s>prastāra</s>).
Having made it square,
with bright grid-lines,
one should make forty-nine
cells, equal and auspicious.
Seated on a half-quarter seat,
with a dot at the end of the five groups,
with the head split by the topknot —
[the syllable] called <s>kaṣa</s>, in the central cell.
In the cells standing in the intermediate and cardinal directions,
beside it, in the eight outer [cells],
one should place the <s>yaśa</s>-group [of letters], O <s>Devī</s>,
in the northeast and so on, in that order.
In the cells from the southeast onward,
the four neuter [syllables];
from the northeast onward, O <s>Devī</s>,
one should place the twelve seed-syllables.
In the cells of the third row,
in the fourth, twenty-five [syllables];
in the cells from the northeast onward,
one should place the seed-syllables in sequence.
Having thus laid out the grid
with vowels and consonants, O Beautiful One,
the sixteen seed-syllables also
one should extract in proper order.
Having first arranged the <s>ka</s>-series row,
in order, both inverted and combined,
with the seed-syllable of the eleventh cell,
conjoined [to form] the twenty-five —
this is known as the <s>ātmatattva</s> (self-principle);
the one called <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) is the thirty-fourth;
the <s>Śivatattva</s> (Śiva-principle), O Goddess,
is conjoined in the thirtieth cells.
This triad of principles
and the placing have been set forth;
all, conjoined with <s>bindu</s> (dot),
are to be placed in proper order.
Herein lies the <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment), O <s>Devī</s>,
to be known by supreme practitioners;
the first seed-syllable is said to be
that which stands in the twenty-fifth cell.
The seed-syllable in the fourteenth cell
is declared to be the second;
the third stands in the eighth cell;
the fourth is the source of <s>bindu</s> (dot).
That which stands in the twenty-fourth cell
is said to be the fifth seed-syllable.
The seed-syllables of the gods and goddesses
have been determined in proper order.
With the time-bound wind seed-syllables,
conjoined with the desired <s>kalā</s> (digit),

children.translated_text: with half-moon, <s>bindu</s>, and topknot,
resembling [each other] in sequence —
having extracted the five seed-syllables,
they have been told to you in order, O <s>Devī</s>;
the five immutable seed-syllables
are remembered as <s>kūṭa</s> (summit), O Fair-faced One.
Having practiced the five seed-syllables,
which grant the fruit of all desires,
I shall declare the worship
that bestows all <s>siddhis</s>.
First, the ritual purification of the hands
should be done in this manner;
and by the method to be described,
the binding of directions and purification must be done.
The binding of directions is [done] with the destruction-weapon (<s>saṃhārāstra</s>),
preceded by breath-control (<s>prāṇāyāma</s>);
with three <s>prāṇāyāmas</s>, O <s>Devī</s>,
one should purify oneself.
Having exhaled, one should release the breath,
and drawing in new [air], one should fill [the body];
retention is called <s>kumbhaka</s> —
this is declared as <s>prāṇāyāma</s>.
Having meditated on the seed-syllable of the fire of destruction,
radiant like the fire at the end of the age,
the <s>mantra</s>-adept should place it on the sole of the foot,
great and surrounded by a garland of flames.
One should burn one's own body
and then flood it with water;
having burnt the material body,
standing like a heap of ashes,
then with streams of nectar
one should visualize the <s>vidyā</s>-body (knowledge-body),
with the supreme <s>praṇava</s> (Oṃ)
flowing down upon the crown, face downward,
conjoined with the nectar of <s>Varuṇa</s>,
pure as clear crystal,
the seed-syllable known as <s>kaṣa</s>,
conjoined with two <s>rephas</s>,
below conjoined with <s>oṃkāra</s>,
above adorned with <s>bindu</s>;
with this very seed-syllable,
with the head split by the topknot,
by the path of the yoga of concentration (<s>dhāraṇā</s>),
the supreme practitioner should burn;
the <s>mantra</s>-adept should purify the body
of terrible sin and defilement.
One should perform the placing (<s>nyāsa</s>) and touching,
thereby becoming one whose body is the <s>mantra</s>;
having purified the direction-binding ground
and for the purpose of purifying the <s>cakra</s> (ritual circle),
with the destruction-weapon (<s>saṃhārāstra</s>) one should perform
the expulsion of obstacles;
afterwards one should purify the hands —
this method has been declared.
The <s>mantra</s>-adept, having done this according to the prescribed method,
should then commence the ritual action;
before the binding of the jewel-band,
one should place the <s>bharamākhā</s> [elements].
From the thumb to the little finger,
one should place the five seed-syllables;
on whatever joints there are, from the thumb,
on both hands,
the <s>ātmatattva</s> (self-principle) should be placed on the head,
the <s>vidyātattva</s> (knowledge-principle) on the second,
the <s>Śiva</s> [-principle] should be given to the third —
for all <s>siddhis</s>, O Beautiful One.
Below is the <s>ātmatattva</s>,
the <s>vidyātattva</s> in the middle,
the <s>Śivatattva</s> should be placed on the head —
on the hands and body, again in order.
Having thus placed the triad of principles
and also the <s>kūṭākṣaras</s> (summit-syllables),
one should again place
the higher seed-syllables, O Fair-faced One.
And having placed the weapon (<s>astra</s>),
radiant like sparks,
having concealed with <s>māyā</s>,
one should restrain with the goad (<s>aṅkuśa</s>).
Then, having formed the <s>yonimudrā</s>,
one should make the entire body <s>sakala</s> (with parts);
this touching-ritual (<s>ālabhana</s>)
has been declared to you, O <s>Devī</s>.
Having interlocked the thumbs
of both hands,
the index finger of the left hand
the wise one should extend and then curve.
This is declared as the restraining [<s>mudrā</s>],
the <s>mudrā</s> of the goad (<s>aṅkuśa</s>);
in acts of subjugation and attraction,
it should be employed by the supreme practitioners.
The index finger, middle finger,
and ring finger of the right [hand],
crossing over the three of the left,
with the two thumbs well-positioned
below — this is declared to be the complete [<s>mudrā</s>];
and the little finger of the right [hand],
between the index finger and thumb —
is proclaimed as the <s>yonimudrā</s> (womb-seal).
The first seed-syllable on the crown of the head, then the second
on the circle of the face,
another above the waist, and then
the fourth from the knees to the waist,
and another from the feet to the knees,
with outstretched hands in sequence.
Thus by the seed-syllable the body
is liberated — there is no doubt here.
From showers of great thunderbolts and stones,
from the terror of thieves and wild beasts,
one is always freed from diseases
that are death-like and difficult to overcome,
from snake-venom, poison, weapons,
fever, leprosy, consumption, and the like —
one is freed, there is no doubt here,
even if one be a sinful man.
Having smeared a clean place,
secluded and free from people,
as before, having drawn a beautiful
<s>maṇḍala</s> (ritual diagram) the span of a hand,
therein a lotus with four petals,
with a pericarp of all colors —
white, red, yellow, and black —
placed on the petals beginning from the east,
the <s>mantrī</s> (mantric practitioner) should place <s>Jayā</s> first,
and <s>Tumburu</s> upon the pericarp,
seated in the lotus posture,
with hand raised in the gesture of granting boons,
four-faced, eight-armed,
four-bodied, three-eyed,
wearing a serpent as sacred thread,
holding a trident, bearing a mace,
with a marvelous crown,
bearing the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
the beloved god of the <s>Śaktis</s> (divine powers),
resplendent with noose and goad in hand,
with a divine garment and parasol,
adorned with divine garlands, fillets, and ointments —
one should always meditate upon the god of gods,
resplendent as ten million suns.
Resembling the fruit of the milky ocean,
wearing a tiger-skin as sacred thread,
mounted upon a corpse, four-faced,
bearing a mace and shield,
with divine garment and parasol,
adorned with necklace and armlets —
one should meditate on <s>Jayā</s>, goddess of gods,
blazing with her own radiance.
Facing the god, the <s>mantrī</s> [should visualize her]
with smiling, wide-open eyes,
resplendent as a pomegranate blossom,
radiant as a firefly,
with hand raised holding a bow, terrible,
fond of fish, meat, and wine,
the goddess seated upon an owl,
adorned with necklace and armlets,
with a red garment and parasol —
one should remember <s>Vijayā</s>, granter of <s>siddhi</s> (supernatural accomplishment).
Resembling mineral gold,
fond of yellow garlands and garments,
the goddess bearing a bell and skull-staff,
mounted upon a horse, of great strength,
radiant as ten thousand suns,
adorned with all ornaments —
meditating on <s>Jayantī</s>, one swiftly
attains abundant <s>siddhi</s>.
Resembling split collyrium,
radiant as the darkness of night,
clad in black silk,
adorned with pearls and gems,
mounted upon a divine aerial chariot,
bearing a mace and shield,
with great roars and thunderous sounds —
one should meditate on <s>Aparājitā</s> (the Unconquered).
Or [one should visualize] <s>Gāyatrī</s>, reciting
and adorned with crystal gems,
singing the <s>Ṛg</s>, <s>Yajus</s>, <s>Sāma</s>, and <s>Atharva</s> [Vedas],
and likewise also
<s>Sāvitrī</s>, of divine form,
delighting in the singing of the <s>Upaniṣads</s>.
Standing foremost among the goddesses, with furrowed brow, one should visualize [the being] called <s>Aṅkuśa</s> (the Goad),
and behind, the king of weapons, with a great tongue displayed and licking,
enraged, terrifying, smeared with the blood, fat, and gore of humans, with stained teeth,
Having thus meditated, O wide-eyed one,
then the worship proceeds.
With offerings of food and eatables,
with scents, flowers, and the like in order,
one should worship [the deity] stationed in the center of the summit,
there in the center, according to the prescribed method.
This very earth with lotus-feet,
on the heart, or in the left hand —
one should always worship mentally,
if one desires <s>siddhi</s>, with concentrated mind.
One should make [the ritual implement] of great conch,
or alternatively of tortoise [shell],
of gold, silver, or copper —
the lineage [vessel] becomes a granter of <s>siddhi</s>.
Or in a scent-<s>maṇḍala</s>,
or in an ash-<s>maṇḍala</s>,
or in a mustard-seed <s>maṇḍala</s>,
or in the <s>maṇḍala</s> of the heart,
or in a safflower <s>maṇḍala</s>,
or in a flower <s>maṇḍala</s>,
or with the pollen of <s>nāgakeśara</s> (iron-wood) flowers,
having drawn the auspicious <s>maṇḍala</s> —
these grant liberation and <s>siddhi</s>,
without a doubt.
Having worshipped duly,
one should offer scent, flowers, and the like.
One should display the <s>yonimudrā</s>,
and at the proper time perform the rites.
When urgent matters arise
that threaten life and property,
the worshipped goddesses protect
the practitioner like a son.
"Here too only the ritual worship has been taught —
what further distinction is there, O Lord?
How, by the mere power of practice,
does <s>siddhi</s> that grants wishes arise?
By mere remembrance alone —
please speak of that.
Show your grace,
if you are gracious, O <s>Maheśvara</s> (Great Lord)."
"Listen with one-pointed mind, O auspicious one,
to the fruit of the ordinary austerity.
Out of affection, [I shall teach] the incomparable
secret, the supreme state.
By means of progressively higher yogas,
the <s>tantra</s> has been taught to you by me.
Having heard this intermediate knowledge,
there arises bliss.
Having spread out the arrangement of syllables as before,
one should extract the group of five seed-syllables.
As before, by the method of sequential yoga,
for the accomplishment of all desires.
The first seed-syllable is the thirty-second,
joined with the nineteenth.
Below that the thirty-fourth —
one should construct [the mantra of] the god of gods.
<s>Jayā's</s> seed-syllable is the seventeenth,
joined with the eleventh.
That itself is declared to be <s>Vijayā</s> [when]

The twenty-fifth, to which the crest belongs,
joined with the eleventh —
this is taught for <s>Ajitā</s> (the Unconquered).
Now hear [the mantra] of the fourth [goddess].
Joined with the eleventh syllable,
the twenty-fifth abiding in <s>Śambhu</s> —
this secret is taught.
It should not be asked of any other.
Granting all desires, O goddess,
is this group of five seed-syllables.
This is indeed the supreme <s>hṛdaya</s> (heart-mantra),
supreme among all <s>tantras</s>.
Whatever rites there may be,
all should be performed with these.
Abiding in the twenty-fifth cell,
joined with the sixteenth —
this is taught as the <s>astra</s> (weapon-mantra)
in this <s>tantra</s>, O virtuous one.
Furthermore, this joined with its seed-syllable,
accompanied by the twentieth —
this is taught as the <s>māyā</s> (illusion-mantra),
of <s>Śiva</s>, of infinite form.
The seed-syllable of the first cell,
joined below with the eighteenth,
abiding in the thirty-eighth cell,
should be placed above it.
This is the <s>aṅkuśa</s> (goad-mantra) for the extraction —
for the restraining of the goddesses.
Endowed with a cluster of <s>bindus</s> (dots),
they should be placed in proper sequence.
Abiding in the twenty-fifth cell,
that itself is the supreme syllable.
Joined with the thirty-ninth,
it is the seed-syllable called <s>Gāyatrī</s>.
This excellent divine seed-syllable
should be employed in consecration rites and the like.
Abiding in the thirty-fourth cell,
joined with the twenty-fifth —
this is taught for all rites,
the seed-syllable called <s>Sāvitrī</s>.
Marked with the half-moon and point, O goddess,
as before.
I shall now teach the application,
by which <s>siddhi</s> quickly arises.
Application is the cause, O goddess;
the textual treatise is not the cause.
Everywhere the treatise is easily obtained,
but application is very hard to find.
<s>Mantras</s> devoid of application
are not considered to be givers of <s>siddhi</s>.
Having placed the yogic arrangement in the heart-lotus,
having meditated upon the five seed-syllables,
having understood the movement of the deity,
then one should commence the rite.
"What is this deity like?
And what is its movement?
How should one know it within the body?
Please speak, O <s>Śaṅkara</s>."
"Between the generative organ and the navel, O goddess,
there is a bulb-like root.
Seventy-two thousand
<s>nāḍīs</s> (subtle channels) are established at the base.
At the region of the navel there is a knot,
and there a lotus is established.
In the middle of the lotus is the pericarp —
there the object [of meditation] is established.
At the end of the hollow of the pericarp,
there is a <s>kalā</s> (subtle power) moving upward.
In the middle of that abides the deity,
resembling the flame of a lamp.
Resembling pure crystal,
radiant as sparks and the sun,
interspersed with water and wind,
of the dimension of a hundredth part of a hair-tip.
Mounted upon the vehicle of the wind,
beyond sound, free from disease,
it is to be apprehended through direct experience —
it moves through the middle of the body.
Going through the middle of <s>Iḍā</s>,
or entering within <s>Piṅgalā</s>,
or entering within <s>Suṣumnā</s> —
this is called the equinox (<s>viṣuva</s>).
<s>Iḍā</s> is said to be on the left,
<s>Piṅgalā</s> is known to be on the right.
Between these two is <s>Suṣumnā</s>,
the effectuator of creation and dissolution.
<s>Iḍā</s> is for pacification and nourishment,
<s>Piṅgalā</s> for death and banishment.
<s>Suṣumnā</s> grants liberation,
following the path of the life-force.
Having meditated on [the deity] within <s>Piṅgalā</s>,
one should visualize it as red in color.
Killing, banishing, and such
rites one should then perform.
Having known [the deity] within the <s>Amṛtā</s> (nectar-channel),
one should meditate on it as snow-white.
Pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and attraction —
such rites one should then perform.
The accomplishment of vows, yoga, and the like
one should perform with the root <s>mantras</s>.
Herein, by mere recitation,
the <s>mantrī</s> accomplishes [the goal] in an instant.
A woman who has not given birth and has died
while still in her youth —
taking the earth from her [burial place],
the skilled one on the left side
should write the name-syllables thereon
situated in the summit of the goddesses.
With blood from the left limb,
the practitioner, observing his vow,
should write a woman thereon
again with cow's yellow pigment (<s>gorocanā</s>).
Striking it with the hair-tips in the natural direction,
one should trample it with the left foot.
At that very moment one quickly summons
a woman from twelve <s>yojanas</s> (leagues) away.
The same is taught for a man —
one should perform it on the right side.
Now one should perform the rite of sorcery (<s>abhicāra</s>)
with fuel-sticks and bones.
Smeared with mustard, poison, and blood,
one should commence the oblation in the cremation ground.
Naked, with hair unbound,
stationed upon three skulls,
one should make the oblation of eight hundred fuel-sticks
at night, the skilled one.
At the end of the oblation, one should visualize <s>Śakra</s> (Indra)
as dark in color,
pierced by a trident,
his head struck by a staff.
The practitioner, in a terrifying form,
enraged, with bloodshot eyes,
can destroy <s>Indra</s> within seven nights —
how much more so a mere human.
With discarded safflower,
one hundred and eight [oblations],
maintaining [the fire] during the three junctions of the night,
one should perform the fire-rite.
Both the target and the practitioner
one should visualize as red in color.
At the end of the oblation, one should meditate on the target
as distressed and swooning.
Struck on the head by the goad,
bound by the noose of <s>māyā</s> (illusion) —
a king or a queen
one brings under control within seven nights.
Taking great flesh (<s>mahāmāṃsa</s>),
mixed with yogurt, honey, and ghee,
with eight thousand oblations —
this is the supreme rite of extraction.
One's own seed-syllable and the target's seed-syllable,
together with the four [syllables] of the five goddesses,
having meditated on [them] as situated within the <s>nāḍī</s>,
unifying them, the skilled one
following the path of the <s>nāḍī</s>,
should cause [them] to enter the body of the target.
By this very application,
one brings the three worlds under control.
Now one should perform the rite of banishment (<s>uccāṭana</s>)
against enemies proud of their strength.
Dried neem leaves
and the tips of banners,
human hair, cremation-ground ash,
the tip-feathers of a crow's wing,
pungent oil, poison, and blood —
mixing with these, one should offer oblation.
Having fetched fire from a <s>caṇḍāla</s> (outcaste),
one should kindle it with funeral-pyre wood.
Within three nights one banishes [the target],
who abandons relatives, friends, and kinsmen.
On the palm of the left hand, having meditated
on the full orb of the moon,
joined with the five seed-syllables —
one should show that hand to the [target] person.
By seeing it, even those intent on killing
come under control.
Whomever one touches with that hand
comes to servitude.
Likewise, on the right hand
one should place the disc of the sun.
Whomever one touches or shows it to —
even friends become enemies.
Taking a crow perched on a neem tree,
brought down by an outcaste,
with these seed-syllables reversed,
anointed with oil, offered on the funeral pyre,
that ash, smeared with poison and blood,
at the dark fortnight's end, of one wearing red garments —
having recited over it a thousand times
with the five seed-syllables in reverse order,
whomever one touches with that ash
wanders the earth like a crow,
despised by all people,
even if he were equal to <s>Śakra</s> (Indra).
As in oneself, so in the target —
one should place the sixteen seed-syllables.
Resembling the <s>javā</s> (hibiscus) flower,
one should visualize these two.
With wings of red vermilion (<s>hiṅgulaka</s>),
radiant as lac juice,
both the target and the practitioner
situated within the enclosure of a lotus,
the goad in the target's secret part,
and the staff in one's own secret part,
resembling safflower-dyed red,
entwined by the thread of <s>māyā</s> (illusion),
for five nights or three nights,
silent, having mastered meditation,
one quickly brings under control
a king proud and arrogant.
A deceased <s>brāhmaṇa</s> woman —
one should take her rag-cloth.
Having taken it on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight,
with burning coals produced from that,
the name interspersed with the <s>bījas</s> (seed syllables),
in whosever house
it is buried, that person swiftly
goes to the abode of <s>Yama</s> (death).
Then, one who is devoted to the <s>vidyāvrata</s> (vow of knowledge),
adorned with fame and other virtues,
is accomplished through this procedure,
and dies without any doubt.
With <s>gorocanā</s> (cow's gallstone pigment) indeed,
one whose name is interspersed
with these <s>bījas</s> (seed syllables) combined together,
the wise one should write it and cast it in.
A vessel filled with honey and ghee —
one should recite a hundred times quickly.
Even for one desiring liberation, through this <s>astra</s> (weapon mantra),
<s>śānti</s> (peace) and <s>puṣṭi</s> (prosperity) arise.
Consecrated a hundred times with water also,
thereby one is always liberated.
With fuel-sticks for destroying disease,
one who is extremely afflicted by disease,
with one hundred and eight
<s>āhutis</s> (oblations), there is no doubt —
with milk-soaked offerings, O <s>Deveśī</s> (Goddess),
the sick one is freed from disease.
He who constantly offers oblations,
whatever wealth is in his house,
even though expenditure is made daily,
it attains inexhaustibility.
Through constant <s>japa</s> (recitation) at the proper time,
one becomes dear to all.
Radiant and endowed with strength,
he is not afflicted by fears.
One desiring prosperity should offer <s>śrīphala</s> (bilva fruit),
and a lotus drenched in ghee and honey.
With one <s>lakṣa</s> (hundred thousand), one gains great wealth;
the <s>mantrī</s> (mantra practitioner), with two <s>lakṣas</s>,
with three <s>lakṣas</s>, becomes lord of the earth,
having conquered enemies, certainly.
One desiring all things should offer sesame;
one shall obtain it, there is no doubt.
With a single <s>lakṣa</s>, O <s>Deveśī</s>,
that <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner) who has conquered his senses,
with cast-off human flesh,
or with the meat of a goat,
through offering a <s>lakṣa</s> quickly,
whatever is desired, that one obtains.
With the milk of a black cow, together with
human flesh mixed with rice grains,
one should offer <s>pāyasa</s> (milk-rice) into the mouth of a corpse,
tirelessly,
until the <s>preta</s> (dead one) rises up
and says, 'What shall I do?'
Whatever is desired should be requested,
and it shall be obtained, O illustrious one.
<s>Guḍikā</s> (magic pills), <s>añjana</s> (magical collyrium), <s>pādukā</s> (magical sandals),
or buried treasure, or sovereignty itself,
the rite of destroying <s>Śakra</s> (Indra),
<s>pādalepa</s> (foot-ointment) and <s>rasāyana</s> (elixir of life) —
having granted one of these requested things,
it departs and not otherwise.
A woman who has died violently,
from her one should take a finger-ring,
consecrating it with these <s>bījas</s> (seed syllables)
in forward order, a hundred
and eight times, the knower of <s>mantras</s>
should intersperse the name of the target.
To whichever woman he gives it, she remains under his power —
thus acts the supreme <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner).
He attracts her swiftly,
even if she were equal to <s>Urvaśī</s>,
even from a distance of a hundred
<s>yojanas</s> (leagues), it is accomplished.
For a man, O <s>Devī</s> (Goddess),
one who is arrogant, O illustrious one —
taking crow's flesh
mixed with neem oil,
establishing the <s>śmaśāna</s> (cremation ground) fire,
one should perform the rite with <s>śigru</s> (drumstick tree) wood.
One should offer oblations for seven nights
in whose name the <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner) performs —
that person becomes hated in the world.
This is the supreme <s>vidveṣaṇa</s> (enmity-causing rite).
Now I shall declare something beyond this,
this wondrous secret,
knowing which, O <s>Maheśānī</s> (great Goddess),
one attains abundant <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment).
Through application at the proper time,
<s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment) is proclaimed in the <s>tantras</s>.
Therefore the <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner) should perform
his rituals at the proper time.
Meditating first on the <s>bījapañcaka</s> (five seed syllables)
situated in the heart-lotus of the target,
one should perform worship mentally,
with the proper steps (?),
then one should veil the target with <s>Māyā</s> (illusion),
both within and without.
With the stalk of the <s>Māyā</s>-lotus,
one should bring the target, enveloped.
Then, placing him face downward,
loosened by the <s>Māyā</s> <s>tattva</s> (principle of illusion),
again having established that,
the supreme <s>sādhaka</s> faces him.
That which should be placed at first (?),
the <s>bījapañcaka</s> (five seed syllables) upon the target.
The <s>mantrī</s> (mantra practitioner), having enveloped that with <s>Māyā</s>,
should then recite eight hundred times,
combined with the syllables of the target's name,
established upon his awakened seat.
Thus, O <s>Devī</s>, swiftly then,
with hair fallen from knees and head,
attracted by this procedure,
the great target becomes a servant.
Beyond this I shall now declare
the liberation of one who is bound or obstructed,
and how one destroys <s>Śakra</s> (Indra's weapon) —
hear that procedure.
Meditating on the <s>bījapañcaka</s> (five seed syllables)
situated within the heart-lotus of the target,
one should perform worship as before,
through the <s>suṣumnā</s> channel's fire-exit (?),
the <s>mantrī</s> should then place the <s>saṃhārāstra</s> (weapon of destruction)
upon the head of <s>Tumburu</s>,
and then with the <s>Devīs</s> (Goddesses),
the knower of <s>yoga</s> should envelop the target.
There, upon the head, with that very
blazing fire-radiance,
having seen him mentally, again
fallen unconscious and distressed upon the ground,
binding him in the heart with the <s>aṅkuśa</s> (hook),
one should bring him near oneself.
Then placing him face downward,
the tormented one should vomit blood.
Afterwards, upon his heart
the <s>bījapañcaka</s> (five seed syllables) should be placed.
Having extracted the target's name thus,
interspersed with the <s>saṃhārāstra</s> (destruction weapon mantra),
thus, with its protection removed,
and having risen forth (?), then
one should recite eight thousand times,
surrounded by garlands of flames.
Then through this ritual action,
by that very method,
the target goes to destruction —
death in its final form (?) causes him to tremble.
Thus has been told, O <s>Devī</s>,
in summary, as before,
how one destroys <s>Śakra</s> (Indra's weapon),
and liberation from bondage and obstruction.
Blazing with great fury,
one should undertake this procedure.
When the deity is in the <s>suṣumnā</s>,
moving of its own accord,
meditating on it as situated within the <s>suṣumnā</s>,
one should visualize it as red in color.
<s>Vidveṣa</s> (enmity), <s>uccāṭana</s> (eradication), and other
rites should then be performed.
Of the deity of the <s>bījapañcaka</s> (five seed syllables),
conjoined with the intervals of the <s>vargas</s> (letter-groups),
the <s>yāga</s> (worship) ending with the last letter, in seclusion —
this has always been kept secret by me.
Now, for the accomplishment of all tasks,
listen, O <s>Suvrate</s> (one of good vows).
With safflower powder mixed
with rice flour,
with ash, with sandalwood,
or with <s>nāgakeśara</s> (Mesua ferrea) pollen,
and with various fragrant substances,
one should draw with full concentration.
Within the interior of the <s>varga</s> (letter-group) diagram,
one should place a four-petaled lotus.
There, the <s>Devīs</s> (Goddesses) along with their brothers,
should be worshipped in the <s>bījapañcaka</s> (five seed syllables).
Thus, merely by being worshipped,
they become givers of all desires always.
They become perpetually
bestowers of <s>dharma</s> (righteousness), <s>kāma</s> (desire), <s>artha</s> (wealth), and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).
Having thus performed the <s>yāga</s> (worship) to completion,
one should then recite three <s>lakṣas</s> (three hundred thousand).
Then one attains <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment),
even a slayer of a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> — it is not otherwise.
Whatever desire is conceived in the mind,
from that time onward one obtains it.
Beyond this I shall declare
the supreme method of <s>japa</s> (recitation).
The <s>mantrī</s> (mantra practitioner), seated in a single posture,
having performed the <s>yāga</s> (worship), knowing the proper procedure,
with one-pointed mind and serene self,
holding the <s>akṣasūtra</s> (rosary) in the left hand,
should always perform the practice of <s>japa</s> (recitation).
Hear now a further distinction:
one desiring <s>vaśya</s> (subjugation) should perform <s>japa</s>
interspersed in forward order
with these <s>bījas</s> (seed syllables) according to proper method,
conjoined with the syllables of the target's name.
One should know the proper time therein;
<s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment) proceeds from timing.
For <s>māraṇa</s> (death-dealing), with reversed order,
the target's name placed first.
For <s>vidveṣa</s> (enmity) also, with reversed order,
one should employ it ending with <s>phaṭ</s>.
For <s>māraṇa</s> (death-dealing), with reversed order,
ending with <s>hūṃ phaṭ</s> (?),
with <s>oṃ svāhā</s> and <s>namaḥ</s> endings
for <s>vaśya</s> (subjugation) and <s>ākarṣaṇa</s> (attraction) rites.
One should offer oblations in this very manner;
the skilled one should perform everything thus.
<s>Namaskāra</s> (salutation) is used at the end of <s>japa</s>,
<s>Svāhā</s> is prescribed for <s>homa</s> (fire offering).
Garlic smeared with one's own blood
should be offered in counter-oblation for <s>māraṇa</s> (killing).
For <s>uccāṭana</s> (eradication), crow feathers;
for <s>vaśya</s> (subjugation), one should offer <s>jāti</s> (nutmeg/jasmine).
For <s>vidveṣa</s> (enmity), <s>śleṣmātaka</s> and <s>śigru</s> (drumstick tree)
should be offered without hesitation.
For <s>ākarṣaṇa</s> (attraction), <s>bakula</s> flowers
should be offered by the skilled one.
All these are prescribed for the <s>yāga</s> (worship),
for the knower of time, O illustrious one.
By whom time is truly known,
by him <s>Sadāśiva</s> is known.
When <s>Sadāśiva</s> is fully known,
<s>sādhaka</s>s (practitioners) attain <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment).
The <s>kālatattva</s> (principle of time) should be understood;
from that <s>tattva</s> (principle), <s>siddhi</s> proceeds.
Those devoid of <s>tattva</s> (principle) knowledge do not succeed,
<s>sādhaka</s>s (practitioners), even with great effort.
Therefore, with all effort,
the wise ones know the <s>kālatattva</s> (principle of time).
When the time of practice is void,
<s>sādhaka</s>s (practitioners) do not succeed here.
Therefore, the practice and the time
should be understood with effort, without neglect.
How is that time to be known,
which you have spoken of, O Lord?
Without time, I consider all to be false,
everything indeed, O <s>Śaṅkara</s>.
Hear, O <s>Devī</s>, the supreme secret,
the embodiment of the <s>kālatattva</s> (principle of time).
Knowing which, with ease,
<s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment) arises for <s>mantrī</s>s (mantra practitioners).
Twenty-two thousand
and sixteen hundred should be known,
through the twenty-four transits,
in the coming and going across twelve finger-breadths.
As in the body, O <s>Devī</s>,
it abides as both <s>sakala</s> (with parts) and <s>niṣkala</s> (without parts),
so I shall declare the <s>Haṃsa</s> (the breath/soul),
for the benefit of <s>sādhaka</s>s (practitioners) indeed.
The feet, the anus, the generative organ,
the hands, and the organ of speech likewise,
hearing, touch, sight, tongue,
and the nose as well —
earth, water, fire,
wind, and space,
sound, touch, form,
taste, and smell likewise,
<s>manas</s> (mind), <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego),
<s>avyakta</s> (the unmanifest) and <s>puruṣa</s> (the self) likewise —
these twenty-five <s>tattvas</s> (principles)
the wise know to be in the body.
By these, which serve as the support,
the supported one is always meditated upon.
The support is called the 'city' (<s>pura</s>),
and the <s>puruṣa</s> (self) is called the supported.
Situated in the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
ever upward-moving, eternal in nature,
of the <s>niṣkala</s> (partless) deity,
again the abode is the <s>ādhāra</s> (support).
That <s>Puruṣa</s> (self), both support and supported,
<s>niṣkala</s> (partless), the supreme <s>Śiva</s>,
the body enclosed in six sheaths,
consisting of the twenty-five <s>tattvas</s> (principles),
endowed with the ten <s>vāyus</s> (vital breaths),
the city pervaded by the <s>nāḍīs</s> (channels),
the body possessing the three <s>guṇas</s> (qualities),
conjoined with all deities —
presided over by Him, O <s>Devī</s>,
it revolves like a wheel.
Just as all the host of stars,
the circle of planets and <s>nakṣatras</s> (lunar mansions),
all that, presided over by <s>Dhruva</s> (the pole star),
revolves while remaining motionless,
so too the body of the deity,
which is the entire host of <s>bījas</s> (seed syllables),
knowing it to be presided over by <s>Śiva</s>,
one attains <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment) in the <s>tantra</s>.
Triply curved, with a coiled form,
endowed with the sixth vowel,
the <s>Śakti</s> (power), pierced by the <s>bindu</s> (drop/point),
abiding in the body, of the nature of all parts.
Her radiant flame-tip is subtle,
resembling a lotus fiber-thread.
She should be known as having the form of light;
at her end, again, is <s>Śiva</s>.
From the letter <s>a</s> to the letter <s>kṣa</s>,
the universe up to the world of <s>Brahmā</s>,
in this, everything arises,
and therein dissolution occurs.
This deity is supreme, subtle,
established as both support and supported.
At the <s>ayana</s> (solstice) and at the <s>viṣuva</s> (equinox),
is the cause of the fiery and the immortal.
When situated on the <s>Vāruṇa</s> (lunar/left) path,
moving through the middle of <s>Iḍā</s>,
resembling snow, jasmine, and moon,
it should be known for auspicious rites.
Resembling twelve suns,
when situated within <s>Piṅgalā</s>,
resembling the dawn-red fire,
one should employ it for <s>raudra</s> (fierce) rites.
When in the <s>Suṣumnā</s>, O deity,
it flows in a pacified state,
this is the path of <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), O <s>Devī</s>,
having the form of light, transcendent and immanent.
This deity is both the goal
and the embodiment of the <s>kālatattva</s> (principle of time).
For the benefit of the <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner),
the supreme truth has been declared.
All this has been fully explained,
the embodiment of the <s>kālatattva</s> (principle of time).
When situated in the three [channels], in brief,
it grants <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment) in all <s>tantras</s>.
How the ritual depends on the <s>nāḍī</s> (channel) state,
the <s>mantrī</s>s (practitioners) always perform —
that I shall now declare;
listen, O <s>Varānane</s> (beautiful-faced one).
<s>Iḍā</s> and <s>Piṅgalā</s>,
these two <s>nāḍīs</s> (channels) are declared.
Through which the deity always moves
and gradually returns,
those rites pertaining to the self,
the Lord performs when they are employed.
He himself performs the ritual action
through the application of <s>bīja</s> (seed syllable) and <s>nāḍī</s> (channel).
This time has been declared
endowed with the three aspects (?).
What resides in the body has been told, O <s>Devī</s>;
the <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner), endowed with the seasons,
having known both time and <s>tattva</s> (principle),
should then commence the ritual action.
<s>Śāntika</s> (pacification) and <s>pauṣṭika</s> (prosperity) rites,
as well as <s>vidveṣa</s> (enmity) and <s>uccāṭana</s> (eradication),
<s>vaśya</s> (subjugation) and <s>ākarṣaṇa</s> (attraction) — one should perform these
if one knows the proper time.
Benign rites at the benign time,
fierce rites at the fierce time should be performed.
A ritual performed at the wrong time
becomes fruitless for the <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner).
Therefore, with all effort,
one should perform rituals at the proper time.
One's own blood, <s>gorocana</s> (cow-bile pigment),
and likewise <s>sindūra</s> (vermilion),
mixed with safflower powder,
combined with curd, honey, and ghee,
with <s>khadira</s> (catechu) wood, red fuel-sticks,
or else with red sandalwood —
having smeared these, the <s>mantrī</s> should offer oblations;
within seven days he brings the target under control.
Having made an image of salt,
the wise one [should recite] one hundred times with consecrated [mantras]
Beginning from the feet, oblations should be offered
until they reach eight hundred
At the three junctions of the day, with concentrated mind,
one should bring about infallible subjugation
Having made an image from sand,
one should anoint it with <s>tryūṣaṇa</s> (the three pungents)
The images being fully complete,
with thorns born of passion,
the skilled one should pierce the feet and the secret parts
and the forehead;
and in the pair of breasts—before the goddesses
one should bury [the image]
Face-down, with limbs smeared
with mustard and salt,
with the blood of a left-handed [person's] nose,
pierced through with name-mantras,
having written [the name], one should place it upon the heart
and kindle a fire above;
mustard and salt also
the wise one should offer eight hundred oblations
At the three junctions of the day, within seven days
one may bring the three worlds under control.
With clay released from a potter's wheel,
an image should be fashioned
Having pierced it with those same thorns
placed in their proper positions, the <s>mantrin</s> (practitioner)
in the vulva or in the phallus—
eight hundred mantras with proper [recitation]
one should thread through the secret region
while always reciting the mantra;
within seven days one will bring under control
a woman or even a man
Having fashioned a peg from human bone,
four finger-widths [in length],
having inscribed a milk-tree [image] on the vulva,
one should then drive in the peg at the phallus
The target will become a eunuch—
an unfailing result, without doubt.
By extracting [the peg], liberation is obtained;
in this matter no deliberation is needed
<s>Madhūka</s> (Madhuca indica), white lotus,
<s>rocanā</s> (yellow orpiment), <s>nāgakeśara</s> (Mesua ferrea),
<s>tagara</s> (Valeriana wallichii) and fine cardamom,
and <s>añjana</s> (collyrium)—in equal portions
Having ground [these] by a maiden,
and performing the ritual sacrifice as prescribed,
having recited one thousand and eight hundred [times],
then by recitation in the offering,
one becomes visible in all worlds
as equal to <s>Kāmadeva</s> (the god of love) himself.
One may wander the entire earth;
in this matter no deliberation is needed
<s>Mañjiṣṭhā</s> (Indian madder) and <s>kunduru</s> (frankincense),
and the two <s>haridrā</s> (turmeric and tree turmeric) should be ground;
having ground [them] according to the earlier procedure,
one should then smear the secret parts
When the time for sexual union arises,
the husband will become a slave.
The root of <s>meṣalocana</s> (Mucuna pruriens),
prepared in milk with a woolen cloth,
the <s>mantrin</s> should consecrate it in a cremation ground
at night, with firewood from that place;
one should rub the body with skull-bowls,
wearing a covering of red garments
This anointing is indeed fearless,
like a thunderbolt, comparable to a goad.
One may eat [it] or show it to anyone—
released from the goad of desire,
a man comes under control,
or a woman proud with passion.
Taking clay from an anthill,
one should fashion a bull
With thread spun by a maiden,
one should pierce its nose;
or with lotus fiber,
smeared with red sandalwood,
having worshipped with red flowers,
one should lead all [the target] to [oneself];
one should write the name of the target
with one's own blood on the bull's belly
Having placed it in the hollow of a <s>śrīvṛkṣa</s> (sacred fig tree),
one should thus subjugate the target.
With that same clay, a ram
the knower of mantras should always fashion
With thread from the ram itself, the nose
the pure one should pierce as before;
having placed it before the goddesses,
one should shake its nose
Whatever desire one makes known,
that the <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner) obtains.
These are the excellent practices, O <s>Devī</s>,
that I have declared to you
The sacrifice performed in the belly of the syllables
grants the fulfillment of all desires.
Likewise, what is placed in the womb,
should be employed for killing
Having written with cow's <s>rocanā</s> (bezoar),
one should employ [it] in the same manner;
one can render [the target] mute among kinsmen—
one can silence even the lord of speech
It is said to constantly attract;
worshipped in the belly of the syllable 'ā',
for great men and excellent women,
through recitation and chanting,
worship guided by the goad of knowledge
quickly [accomplishes] in most matters;
in states of madness and in terrible [situations]
one should accomplish [the rite] with the syllable form
Through the sacrifice in the belly of the syllable 'e',
it becomes a granter of wealth;
and placed within the syllable 'va',
[it is effective] in the rite of subjugation
It grants <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, and <s>mokṣa</s>,
and increases prosperity and radiance;
it becomes fixed, O <s>Devī</s>,
when worshipped in the midst of the syllable 'haṃ'
For routing armies,
[the mantra] placed in the belly of the syllable 'bha';
it becomes certainly and quickly
most excellent for conferring safety
For killing, it should be employed
stationed at the end of 'phaṭ';
they produce enmity
when stationed in the belly of the syllable 'ja'
It would cause the destruction of the enemy's family
stationed at the end of 'hūṃ phaṭ';
for minor works,
[it is placed] in the belly of the syllable 'ya'
I shall now describe the placement upon the body,
O Supreme Goddess, which is impenetrable;
having placed the instruments directly
upon the five great elements,
having placed the triad of principles upon the body,
preceded by <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control),
one should place [them] on the body, O <s>Devī</s>,
in the order previously stated
Having concealed with <s>māyā</s> (illusion),
one should restrain with the goad;
having formed the <s>yoni mudrā</s> (womb seal), then afterwards
the <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner), well-concentrated,
the <s>mantrin</s>, with salutation upon his own body,
by the ritual action prescribed in the <s>kalpa</s> (manual),
should perform all actions—
then success [is certain], without doubt
In the subsequent and primary tantras,
one should perform the action prescribed in the <s>kalpa</s>;
or one who recites twelve hundred thousand [times]
according to the proper procedure,
then the goddesses together with their companions
stand before the <s>sādhaka</s>
and grant the desired boon—
that state which transcends the three [worlds]
This fivefold seed-syllable indeed
should not be given to just anyone;
pervaded by the quality-transcending [syllable] at the end of the class,
this is truly the fivefold seed
Having first performed [the rites] in this manner,
having understood the procedure thus,
the wise one should sow the seeds,
then commence the ritual action
One who knows this procedure,
even if lacking in all marks [of distinction],
even if associated with sins,
shall become a partaker of the fruit of <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment)
Of that called the quality-transcending [syllable] at the end of the class,
this too is considered supreme;
it is the heart of the gods and goddesses—
the single syllable beyond this
Where the goddesses with their companions
are established in their assembled form—
no mantra superior to this
exists in the three worlds
It should be guarded with great effort—
this essence of the tantra, most difficult to obtain;
even by me it has been guarded, O <s>Devī</s>,
by the omniscient one, at all times
Having bound my inner resolve—?
that which was spoken by the Lord,
by you also, in this same way,
it must be protected with effort
This is the secret wish-fulfilling gem,
devoid of vows and external practices;
merely by remembrance,
having properly understood, by degrees,
by the very method of syllable-sacrifice,
in the order previously stated,
success is achieved—there is no doubt here—
all desires of the <s>mantrins</s> [are fulfilled]
Pacification, prosperity,
enmity and expulsion likewise,
subjugation, attraction, and destruction—
all is accomplished for the practitioner
With semen in the all-auspicious [maṇḍala],
and in the great bewildering [rite] as well—
churned and spoken, O <s>Devī</s>,
extracted like ghee from curd
Having examined the disciple by the guru—
[one who is] a worshipper of guru, deity, and fire—
to such a one this tantra should be given,
but not to a reviler or disbeliever
The uninitiated do not attain accomplishment
even if they persist for a hundred <s>kalpas</s> (aeons);
those who have self-appropriated mantras,
atheists, and revilers of the <s>Vedas</s>,
those fallen from their vows,
and corruptors of the tantras,
those intent on harassing gurus,
and destroyers of the essence of tantra—
they are always rejected by the <s>yoginīs</s>,
declared to be violators of <s>dharma</s>.
This is the truth, O <s>Mahādevī</s>,
honored by gods and demons
This indeed is the essence of the tantra,
established therein, in the great doctrine;
by the command of the <s>Bhagavān</s>,
<s>Śiva</s>, the Supreme Self
I have heard, O <s>Mahādeva</s>,
the supreme true nature of the <s>Vīṇā</s>;
the tantra called <s>Vīṇāśikha</s>,
difficult to obtain even among the gods
Of that called the quality-transcending [syllable] at the end of the class,
this too is the supreme;
the single syllable, supremely secret,
the bestower of enjoyment and liberation
It has been concealed by you, O Lord,
the essential [teaching], O <s>Maheśvara</s>;
that knowledge born from <s>Śiva</s>,
obtained through difficult <s>tapas</s> (austerity)—
bestow your grace, O Lord of Gods,
where accomplishment is firmly established;
in the terrible <s>Kali Yuga</s> that has arrived,
full of distress and many sins,
for those who have taken refuge in all streams [of tradition],
so that swift accomplishment [may come] to people—
bestow your grace, O Lord of Gods;
who else but you can take me across?
Those of little wisdom, of bad intellect,
with minds greatly troubled—
they do not attain the tantra,
nor is it heard in many [versions]
Thus, O Lord, formerly
it was taught by you as guru;
for us also, in brief,
please speak it, O <s>Maheśvara</s>
O you of natural, innate disposition—
why do you ask again and again?
That which was spoken by me before,
accept that well-spoken [teaching]
I shall not ask again;
[but] one question is of great importance:
make clear just once
the grace that pertains to the subtle realm
Listen, O <s>Devī</s>, with attention—
that which is subtler than the subtle, [yet] great,
the practice of all tantras,
the supreme [method] for accomplishing all <s>siddhis</s>
By which, through mere remembrance,
<s>siddhi</s> stands upon the palm of the hand;
no exertion, no vow,
no <s>tapas</s> (austerity), O <s>Maheśvarī</s>—
no fire ritual, no worship even—
through mere remembrance it is declared to grant <s>siddhi</s>;
hear the single syllable, O <s>Devī</s>,
established in the supreme truth
The body, the king of principles,
established in <s>Jātavedas</s> (the fire);
the deity established in the crest—
the <s>bindu</s>-goddess is known as <s>Jayā</s>
And that which is above this, O <s>Devī</s>,
is declared to be the <s>saukara</s> (boar-form);
one should know the thread-deity
and the <s>makāra</s> as the <s>bindu</s>-deity
Thus in fivefold manner, O <s>Devī</s>,
the king of principles is proclaimed;
in the grid of twenty-four,
that which is known as the lord of mantras,
known as the king of principles—
nineteen below is declared;
with the twentieth vowel,
pressed by the <s>bindu</s> above
This single syllable is proclaimed
for your sake, O beautiful-faced one;
the hollow [form], the king of principles,
established in <s>Jātavedas</s>
Above <s>Viṣṇu</s>, with the blazing [syllable],
the wise one should recite three hundred thousand [times];
this [mantra] can attract trees,
animals, birds, and serpents
What concern then for attracting humans
with regard to the method of attraction?
Combined with the eleventh [vowel],
with the king of principles, O fair one,
with the head split by the <s>bindu</s>—
this is declared as the heart [mantra];
the twenty-seventh is declared as the head,
and the thirtieth becomes the crest
The thirty-ninth, O <s>Devī</s>,
is known as the principle of the armor;
combined with the sixteen vowels,
this is proclaimed as the weapon [mantra]
The eye [mantra] has been described, O <s>Devī</s>,
as consisting of twenty syllables;
this single syllable, O <s>Devī</s>,
is declared with its six limbs
<s>Haṃsa</s> joined with <s>māyā</s>, O <s>Devī</s>,
interwoven with the iron-arrow weapon;
with <s>visarga</s>, the secret seed-syllable contained within (?),
ū ī—the accomplisher for humans (?)
ha ra tra produces growth,
<s>māyā</s>, the goad, and the restraints—these
are the hosts of all mantras and so forth
The <s>mantrin</s> should combine [them] in sequence
if one desires longevity for oneself;
having abandoned all else,
one should undertake the collection of mantras
For those who have the self and senses as their support,
one must do this again and again;
endowed with the method of word-meanings,
that which was spoken by me formerly,
that, by this very practice,
should be done by one desiring accomplishment;
one should meditate on [it as] vermillion-colored
for the rite of subjugation and attraction
For killing, [meditate on it as] black-colored,
for enmity, in a crooked form;
for expulsion, smoke-colored,
and white for one desiring prosperity
Like the color of a peacock's neck—
for immobilization, one should always visualize [it thus];
and bearing all colors,
it is indeed [effective] for all desires
One should make an offering of all the senses
to the great lord;
above the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
one should visualize the hollow [space] there
A spark in the form of the pericarp,
having the form of smokeless radiance,
free from smoke and flame,
with brilliance equal to ten million suns
Above that, a subtle flame,
pure, like crystal;
it is always served by disciplined
<s>yogins</s>—the partless, supreme [reality]
Like the form of a spider's thread,
flowing upward, incomparable—
in the middle of that, one should see what has entered
as born from the supreme secret of the <s>Devī</s>
Known as a hundredth part of a hair-tip,
well-established as the support of the <s>vīṇā</s> (lute)—
the supreme <s>yogin</s> should always meditate
on that which is born from the subtle secret
Having first performed the placement,
established both in the complete and external [aspects],
thus, having understood the division of syllables,
one attains <s>siddhi</s> (accomplishment)
The rites of subjugation and attraction—
by speech alone one will accomplish [them];
this is the entirety of the <s>Vīṇāśikhā</s>—
like another wish-fulfilling gem
Having obtained this supreme seed [mantra],
do as you desire
This is the command of the <s>Bhagavān</s>,
ever unfailing.
It should be meditated upon with effort
if one desires <s>siddhi</s> (perfection) for oneself.
Worship (<s>yajana</s>), causing to worship (<s>yājana</s>),
union (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and dissolution (<s>laya</s>) likewise,
the <s>samaya</s>-syllable-seed (<s>samayākṣarabīja</s>),
conjoined with syllable upon syllable (<s>akṣarākṣarayojita</s>) —
this should be guarded by you, O blessed one,
with effort, most firmly.
This secret has been declared
to you out of affection, O discerning one.
Having known this, the knower of <s>mantras</s>
would attain union with <s>Śiva</s> (<s>Śivasāyujya</s>).
Thus one attains dissolution
of women by this method.
The <s>sādhaka</s> (practitioner), having purified the body
by this method,
should place that purified <s>mantra</s>
in the heart-<s>cakra</s> (<s>hṛccakra</s>).
Situated in the center of the lunar sphere (<s>somamaṇḍala</s>),
one should meditate upon it as having the radiance of jasmine and the moon.
They sprinkle with <s>amṛta</s> (nectar)
with [the substance] connected with <s>lāntī</s> (?),
thus the <s>mantra</s>, being nourished,
becomes the bestower of all <s>siddhis</s> (perfections).
Having thus performed the nourishment (<s>āpyāyana</s>),
the discerning one, at the center of the <s>bindu</s>,
one thousand and eight
<s>mantras</s> the knower of <s>mantras</s> should recite.
This indeed is the supreme accomplishment (<s>paramīkaraṇa</s>),
known as the nourishment of the <s>mantra</s>.
The <s>mantra</s>, having become <s>Śiva</s>-like,
would accomplish the entire universe.
Restrained in the solar <s>cakra</s> (<s>sūryacakra</s>),
established in the head,
one should recite it together with the <s>hūṃ</s>-syllable —
this is called the awakening (<s>bodhana</s>).
Situated in the center of the solar disc (<s>ādityacakra</s>),
restrained by fire (<s>vahni</s>),
it burns the <s>mantra</s>, O <s>Devī</s>,
when [the mantra] does not perform its function.
Having meditated upon it as situated in the center of the topknot (<s>śikhā</s>),
one should repeat it a thousand times.
The <s>mantra</s> thus indicated
is the illumination of the secret power (<s>guhyaśakti</s>).
The burning (<s>dahana</s>) should be done with fire,
and one should awaken it with the <s>hūṃ</s>-syllable.
The illumination (<s>dīpana</s>) is in the center of the topknot
for the speakers of <s>mantras</s>.
The sun purifies [the mantra],
nourishment (<s>āpyāyana</s>) is known [to be done] by the moon.
The <s>mantra</s> practitioner, the knower of <s>yoga</s>, should make the <s>mantra</s> <s>Śiva</s>-like
while it is situated in the <s>bindu</s>.
Thus the one whose <s>mantra</s> is purified,
endowed with the moon and the sun,
should always illuminate it with <s>Śakti</s>
— the <s>mantra</s> practitioner should recite with concentration.
At the time of the arising of <s>amṛta</s> (nectar),
the <s>mantra</s> practitioner, with effort and certainty,
quickly brings under control
the entire [universe] — there is no doubt (?).
Whatever <s>māyā</s> (creative power) of <s>mantras</s>
of all [kinds] has been told by me,
the method herein and the sequence —
afterward I shall speak of the method of recitation (<s>japa</s>).
When the time of worship (<s>yajana</s>) has arrived,
with one-pointed mind, concentrated,
seated on the pericarp of the heart-lotus (<s>hṛtpadma</s>),
with mind offered to the deity,
having ascertained the topknot-<s>bindu</s> (<s>śikhābindu</s>),
that <s>mantra</s> established in the heart,
there should be the arrangement of encased syllables (<s>putavarṇa</s>),
without audible utterance.
With a composed mind, undeluded,
with the self established upward in the <s>alā</s> (?),
uninterruptedly, swiftly,
and without delay —
the <s>mantra</s> practitioner should recite the <s>mantra</s> for as long
as the mind does not become fatigued.
My <s>mantra</s>, not [otherwise] obtainable,
is quickly accomplished in due time.
Having performed the recitation, the wise one
should not offer this to another.
The <s>mantra</s> practitioner should endeavor with effort —
understand its true meaning.
The first is declared as pertaining to wind (<s>vāyavī</s>),
the second is known as pertaining to fire (<s>analā</s>),
the third as pertaining to <s>Indra</s> (<s>māhendrī</s>),
and pertaining to <s>Varuṇa</s> (<s>vāruṇī</s>) in the other.
The <s>mantra</s> preceded by <s>oṃkāra</s>,
conjoined with <s>namaskāra</s> at the end,
with the seed-cluster (<s>bījapiṇḍa</s>) in the middle,
endowed with <s>mudrā</s>, one should always worship.
Quickly, the goal and the rite,
enjoyment and pleasure most difficult to obtain,
one should accomplish all mentally
through the application of seed and <s>mudrā</s> (<s>bījamudrā</s>).
The <s>hūṃ</s>-syllable placed at the beginning,
established with <s>namaskāra</s> at the end,
one should expel all evil beings,
demons (<s>daitya</s>), ghosts (<s>bhūta</s>), and seizers (<s>graha</s>) likewise.
Conjoined with <s>oṃkāra</s> at the beginning,
ending with <s>svāhākāra</s>,
this is the application of the fire-rite (<s>agnikārya</s>) —
it quickly accomplishes the goal.
The cluster encased in <s>oṃkāra</s>,
illuminated by the <s>ra</s>-syllable,
one should accomplish mentally through meditation,
for the purpose of desire (<s>kāma</s>), as wished.
The <s>mantra</s> practitioner awakens [even] the sleeping [mantra]
and quickly obtains <s>siddhi</s> (perfection).
<s>Oṃkāra</s> and <s>ra</s>-syllable
and <s>phaṭ</s>-syllable in the middle —
with the class-final cluster in the middle,
one should perform the rite as desired.
<s>Hūṃ</s>-syllable at the beginning and end,
and <s>ha</s>-syllable at the beginning and middle —
reciting, the <s>mantra</s> practitioner should awaken [the mantra],
even if it is sleeping and inert.
<s>Hūṃ</s>-syllable and <s>ra</s>-syllable
and <s>phaṭ</s>-syllable at the beginning and middle —
angered, the <s>mantra</s> practitioner should recite
when [the mantra] does not perform its function.
Having made [the mantra] encased in <s>oṃkāra</s>,
conjoined with <s>namaskāra</s> at the end,
the <s>mantra</s> practitioner should recite the seed-syllable cluster (<s>piṇḍākṣara</s>),
the supreme bestower of all <s>siddhis</s>.
For pacifying (<s>śāntika</s>) and enriching (<s>pauṣtika</s>) rites,
in auspicious and inauspicious [occasions],
there is quick <s>siddhi</s> in invocation (<s>āvāhana</s>)
through the application of oblation-seeds (<s>homabīja</s>).
One should offer in the fire fruit-seeds,
grain-seeds, and grasses,
or with pure milk —
thus the fire-rite (<s>homakarma</s>) has been described.
With honey mixed with ghee,
one should offer sesame (<s>tila</s>), O discerning one.
One should accomplish all rites
with the <s>vaṣaṭ</s>-exclamation while reciting.
For all secret <s>mantras</s>,
one should employ the seed-<s>mudrā</s> (<s>bījamudrā</s>).
This secret, not to be disclosed,
has issued forth from the mouth of <s>Śiva</s>.
Whoever meditates on this constantly
and worships and mentally recites —
that one enjoys abundant pleasures
and attains the state of <s>Īśāna</s> (lordship).
The <s>Vīṇāśikhā</s>, three hundred and fifty [verses], a <s>Yāmala Tantra</s>, is complete.

<s>Ajita</s> — <s>Vaiśānī</s> — fire.
<s>Aparājita</s> — <s>Śūdrāṇī</s> — wind.

D:
The <s>kṣa</s>-syllable is <s>Puruṣa</s> directly; the <s>ma</s>-syllable is known as <s>Prakṛti</s>.
The great [principle] is said to be the <s>ha</s>-syllable; <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> is known as <s>ya</s>.
<s>Oṃkāra</s> is declared as <s>Manas</s> — thus told to you, O <s>Devī</s>, in sequence.

Colophon:
The <s>Vīṇāśikha</s>, a <s>Vāma Tantra</s>, is fully complete. May there be auspiciousness.
